utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I see that both Mr. Hedaraly and Mr. Russo are present. Mr. Hedaraly, are you here in relation with the Witness 3 issue and the photospread?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I'm here for the examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware that, but at least you're here anyhow, so we might find a moment and abuse your presence to have the matter further discussed. I inform the parties that there is a swearing-in ceremony today at 1.30, so we have to stop early. It is my understanding that the swearing-in ceremony takes place in this courtroom, which also might mean we may even have to stop not at 1.29 but even earlier, in order to have the courtroom ready for the swearing-in ceremony. Then, Mr. Hedaraly, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution would like to call Witness 40, Mr. Kosta Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is aware that the Gotovina Defence opposes the admission into evidence of, let me say it briefly, the map and the description given by this witness on how Operation Storm developed militarily. Mr. Hedaraly, you're invited to explore with the witness sources of what he knows and how he knows. We'll then, after that, decide whether these two documents are fit to be admitted into evidence or whether it is a kind of reconstruction which should be done primarily by the Chamber rather than by the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine Your Honour. Just one comment on the objections. From the Prosecution's viewpoint, it is a little odd that the Gotovina Defence produces maps from their trial team; whereas, maps that are produced by the witness are being objected to. I will explore the matter with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, perhaps your team could prepare maps as well, isn't it? Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just it will be briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would rather first say --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'll give you an opportunity to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. Please be seated. Mr. Novakovic, before we start with your examination, there was another matter which was just discussed and which needs another 30 seconds to be dealt with, if could you have some patience. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just so our position is clear, Your Honour, we of course have no problems with the Prosecution putting in maps. However, I would point out that the Prosecution never misses an opportunity when we put in a map to ask for the underlying documents from which we put the map together, and I don't think the Prosecution thus far has allowed to us say, One of our people thinks this is the way it was, so we can tender the map into evidence. Similarly, all we're asking for with this witness is to explore how he knows, on what basis; and if you knows and has some foundation for it, of course then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you have understood that this is the kind of exercise the Chamber invited Mr. Hedaraly to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, you will first be examined by Mr. Hedaraly, and Mr. Hedaraly is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Kosta Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, for the record, could you please also state your date and place of birth?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: 6 December 1949, Bijeljina village, Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could have 65 ter 6026 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, do you recall providing a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in February and April 2001?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that the statement we see on the screen right now; and if we go to the bottom, can we see your signature?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we now could have 65 ter 6027, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Novakovic, do you recall providing another witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in March of 2007?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that the statement that we see on the screen right now, with your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, finally, if we could have 65 ter 6028.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I want to ask you the same question. Do you recall providing a supplemental witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor last month, on 2 and 3 October 2008?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And is that the statement that we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could provide a hard copy of the statements to the witness in his own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, if we can the -- first, let me ask you: Did you have a chance to review these three statements before today?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You showed them to me in the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the third statement, which at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If you could go to paragraph 12, the third sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm going to wait for it appear on the screen for the Judges. That would be page 3 of the document that is on the screen right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The third sentence in paragraph 12 says: "This personnel," we're talking about the personnel in the Senjak barracks, "did include any fighting soldiers." Can you clarify whether you meant that this personnel did include fighting soldiers or whether this personnel did not include any fighting soldiers?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: What is true is that there were no fighting soldiers, combatants among the men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In the Senjak barracks?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the Senjak barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And in paragraph 13, you have also noticed a translation issue. The first line of paragraph 13 in English talks about a storage building in the southern barracks; and in the B/C/S translation, it says the northern barracks. Can you tell the Court which one is accurate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It should read southern barracks. It's obviously a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, apart from these corrections, do these three statements that you reviewed accurately reflect what you said to the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And are the contents of the statements that you reviewed and that you signed true, to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked in those interviews, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would like to have 65 ter 6026, 65 ter 6027, and 65 ter 6028 admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understand that there are no objections against admission of the 92 ter statements. Mr. Registrar, 6026?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 6026 becomes Exhibit number P1092; 6027 becomes Exhibit number P1093; and 6028 becomes Exhibit number 1094.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1092 up to and including P1094 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I also have admitted into evidence 65 ter 6030, which is the attachment to the 2008 statement, the photo of Knin that was marked by the witness in his October 2008 interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand that there are objections against the other attachments, but not against this one. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit P1095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1095 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Registrar, could with he have 65 ter number 6029 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Novakovic, what will come up on the screen is the map that you had provided the Office of the Prosecutor in March 2007 with the various locations of the -- of the Croatian and the army of the RSK troops. Now, can I ask you: What sources did you use to -- first of all, let me ask you: Did you prepare this map yourself?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I prepared it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What sources did you use to include the information that we find on this map?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Let me state, first of all, that I made this map for the purpose of a book I had been working on for ten years now, which portrays the Croatian-Serbian relations. I prepared the map through the use of several methods. I primarily used the sources of the Serbian army of the Krajina, when I was stating the disposition of the Serbian army soldiers which is marked in red here. As far as the units of the Croatian army and the Croatian Defence Council are concerned, I used several sources. One of the sources was General Janko Bobetko's book, "All My Battles." I used the sources of General Spegelj, and of a gentleman, Mr. Baric, who wrote a doctoral thesis on the subject matter. I use some other sources, the Croatian press, and other intelligence sources I had at my disposal. I also used the sources for the sources for the 5th Muslim Corps marked in green on the map, also by drawing upon the sources that I mentioned. I used at least a dozen sources in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we could 65 ter 4685 which is a text that, according to your statement, corresponds to the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Was that also prepared using the same sources you've just described?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I used the same methods there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, I would like to have 65 ter 6029 and 4685 admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, I would first ask some additional questions in relation to this. Mr. Novakovic, you said you used many sources. Did any of these sources ever contradict another source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, no, the sources concerning the Serbian army of the Krajina was something that I was quite familiar, and I was in touch with a lot of the people responsible for these units, i.e., their commanders. I also had personal knowledge since I was a member of the Main Staff. As far as the Croatian sources are concerned, I also consulted several books, written sources. For the most part, the information came from the book, the press, and documents. Though, I would say that General Janko Bobetko's book contained it all; and if you went through the book, you could clearly follow where the units were. These were the indicators that I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this Chamber has not read Mr. Bobetko's book. Is there -- apparently, you rely on this book as being a truthful account of what happened. Did you ever find anything in that book on which you'd say, "Well, it contradicts other sources"? Because I asked you specifically on whether there was any contradiction anywhere, and you said, "Well, mostly not." But could you give an example of where the sources do contradict each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there were such cases when it came to political and other positions. As far as the units themselves were concerned, there was no contradiction, or almost none. The units were correctly portrayed. After all, from intelligence and other sources, one knew what sort of units there were. Just as the Croats knew which units we had, we knew which units they had. We knew their composition pretty well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it is not just about the existence of units, but also where they were located, and, to some extent, also how they moved. But, again, you said: "As far as the units themselves, there was no contradiction, or almost none." Could you give us an example on where you found that rare contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there could be contradiction over political and other issues, issues that were not of a purely military nature. I did not go into such cases in great detail. For the purposes of my book, I felt the indicators were sufficient in order for me to conclude which tactical axes, which particular unit could have acted along, and which axes were covered by which particular unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you said in your previous answer: "As far as the units themselves were concerned," so that is apart from the political positions, "there was no contradiction, or almost none." And I'm exploring with you where you ever found a contradiction, because I want to know what you did when you found such a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in such cases, I would consult other sources. I crossed-referenced my sources in various ways. I had sources at my disposal through contact with different people, but this was not my primary concern in preparing the material. I made a general overview portraying the situation as it was, the balance of powers, and the units involved along the attack axes or our units along defence lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it may not have been your primary concern, but it might be a concern of the Chamber. Can you give us an example of such a contradiction, where you said you had to further consult with other sources, where you cross-referenced your sources in various ways. Could you give us an example on where you had to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't recall it specifically at this time. I used Mr. Bobetko's source as the primary one, then Mr. Spegelj's, Mr. Baric's, and others. And if the information contained in several sources was consistent, I concluded it to be true, especially if it made sense, if it was logical. This was not my primary focus. I was engaged on quite a different type of business.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that, that your focus when you're writing a book is different from perhaps the focus this Chamber may have on hearing your testimony. Did you prepare a list of your sources? Do you have a complete list? Because I don't know whether you are including any footnotes in your book; but then I take it that, if so, reference will be made to your various sources. Do you have a list of them? Because your reference is refer general.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the problem is that I haven't published a book. I have the manuscript on a CD. I have between 90 and 100 books and a great deal of footnotes. My manuscript is on a CD; and if Their Honours are interested, I'd like gladly produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't think the whole of the manuscript, but I'm mainly focussing on the sources. Do you have a separate file in which you list your sources that you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do have a chapter listing all the books and documents that I used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have the CD with you here in The Hague? Is there any way of providing it on a short notice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hedaraly, the last thing you did was to tender the two documents into evidence. Could I hear whether there are any objections or whether there are any further wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Our request would be to see the material of the witness if he has it present, primarily because my objection is that this witness does not have apparently personal knowledge of the matters that he has put on the card; and the sources, thus far, that underlie the map are still unclear to me. Other than reference to one or could books, I will mention that, as far as I know, the specific authors he referenced were themselves not involved in Operation Storm. Mr. Bobetko had been retired by that point. So I would like to check the sources so that can I cross-examine the witness, if necessary, and also to object to admission, if necessary, if it is just a recapitulation of other material. And, finally, our objection, just so the Trial Chamber understands, our objection is also as to what's actually in the map. For that reason, that's why I want to get at where he is getting this information from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just very briefly, I understand the concern and I'm more than happy that the Defence should have a chance to explore the sources, but that should nod be a bar to the admissibility of the document. That would go to the weight of it. And once he has the sources, Mr. Misetic is entitled to cross-examine the witness on the sources, but the foundation which was the objection is not a proper objection at this stage, because the witness prepared it and he told us what the foundation is. Now, if Mr. Misetic disagrees with the foundation of it, it becomes a weight issue, and he can ask question on it, but it doesn't bar the admissibility of map at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my position is that we don't know what the foundation is yet, because we haven't been produced what the footnotes are. As to the book he mentioned, I think, ten sources, of which I think he identified two, maybe three, by name. So we don't know the foundation of this is it, and on top of that, if it is just a recapitulation of other source material --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is apparently is mixed sources, including what he observed himself and other sources, and cross-referenced. Let me just have one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the two documents you've tendered into evidence, that's the map and the description, will be marked for identification for the time being. At the same time, Mr. Novakovic, with the assistance of the Victims and Witness Section, you're invited to give your CD and perhaps write down which are the relevant files on your CD, so that either the CD in its entirety, or at least the file which contains a list of your sources could be copied, could be made available to the parties so that they can further orient themselves on what sources you used. Therefore, a very practical question: Do you have that CD with you in this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So, during the first break, would you be willing to hand that over? I take it that the parties will fully respect the copyright of this witness, so even if he would give the text, that this is just limited for the purposes of this trial and, of course, of it's work product, which, I would say, deserves to be protected even if he would give it to the parties for these limited purposes. Then the Victims and Witness Section, during the first break, will get in touch with you, and if you'd write down for them what the relevant files on the CD are. You know now that with we're not seeking to have access to what you wrote, but mainly we're interested in knowing what sources you used when producing the map and when producing the document, deployment of Serbian Krajina sources shortly before Croatian aggression, as you gave it as its title. Would you be willing to assist us in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. If I may, I'd just like to add something. Perhaps I did not put it sufficiently explicitly when I was talking about it, when I said that I knew the disposition of our forces. Since I was assistant commander in the staff, and although I was not engaged in operational matters but, rather, I dealt with religious and morale affairs, I, as a person from the staff, knew what the disposition of the Croatian forces and their names were. The operational and intelligence organs were in possession of such data. That was not unknown to them. I merely double-checked that with the other sources, i.e., the books. There were no deviations from the original indicators I possessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say, in your capacity as assistant commander in the staff, you had intelligence information from the units of the opposing party in the conflict. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this explanation. You're invited to cooperate with the Victims and Witness Section so that, finally, the relevant files are copied and are put in the hands of the registry, who will then make it available to the parties. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed. We first have to assign numbers to them. First, the map, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 6029 becomes Exhibit number P1096, marked for identification; and 65 ter 4685 becomes Exhibit P1097, also marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They keep that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I read a short summary of the evidence of the witness as contained in the three statements that were admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Kosta Novakovic was a member of the Yugoslav People's Army and subsequently an officer of the Main Staff of the army of the Republika Srpska Krajina, ARSK. Prior to and during Operation Storm, he was the spokesperson of the ARSK based in Knin, and General Mrksic's assistant in charge of information, religious, and legal issues. He was the chief liaison officer between the ARSK, the Croatian authorities, and the international community. Mr. Novakovic was based in Knin for a period of four years between 1991 and August 1995, and frequently visited ARSK military units on the front line. His position allowed him to gain detailed knowledge about the location and composition of ARSK forces and military facilities in the territory of the former RSK. His position also allowed him to gain detailed knowledge about the use of specific buildings and locations in Knin and the number of ARSK soldiers in the town prior to and during Operation Storm. For example, in early August 1995, the northern barracks only housed a total of approximately 30 soldiers who were manning the medical facilities, the kitchen, and the technical workshop. Mr. Novakovic was also present at the meeting of the RSK leadership in the evening of 4 August 1995, when it was decided that the civilian population should be moved to safer areas within the RSK territory. This concludes my summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. I noted that you developed the exact speed in which both interpreters booth and the transcriber were able to follow you, which is certainly appreciated by them. No "vivace" but just "moderade." Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Better late than never, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, let me ask you a few questions regarding your statements. You just heard in my summary I referred to you as the assistant to General Mrksic. Can you clarify for the Court whether you were an assistant commander or a deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is quite a difference. Deputy commander is the Chief of Staff who, in certain situations, has the competencies of the commander. Assistant commander is in charge of a particular area; and as specified in the title, that person is an assistant and has no particular competent in that area. I was an assistant commander for information, religious matters, legal affairs, and a liaison with international organisations. In that respect, I often acted as a spokesperson for the army of Serbian Krajina; and, at a certain point in time, I headed the delegation of the Serbian Krajina during negotiations abroad or in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. Acting as such, I was not in command of any units. I did have, however, certain subordinate formations of mine, which were the army hall of the Serbian Krajina army, the library, the press centres, the editorial room of our military gazette, and, for a short while, the military band, but these were not combat units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to refer to a your first statement P1092. At page 11 of that statement in the English in the second full paragraph, you state -- and I will just read it out for you, and then I will ask you a series of questions on that. It says: "I wish to clarify here that no plans for the evacuation of the population had been made at the RSK level; however, plans were drawn up at the level of municipalities and villages, exclusively for the purpose of protecting the population and moving it to safer areas but only inside RSK. There were never any plans for leaving the territory of RSK." Now, I first want to show you an exhibit, D255, which is a 29 July 1995 document, and it will appear on the screen in front of you in just a few seconds. I want firstly to focus on the top of that document where it says: "Republic of Serbian Krajina, republican civilian protection staff." First, I want you to please tell the Court, briefly, what is civilian protection and what were its responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The civilian protection of the RSK fell under the Ministry of Defence of the RSK as a segment of the ministry. Civilian protection, as an aspect of an organised way to protect the population, is something that was common to all armed forces in the former state. Its primary goal was to protect the population. That was the raison d'etre of civil protection, to protect the population from various dangers, be it war, emergency situations, natural disasters, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if we go to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and that's the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You can see that the author of this is a person called Dusko Babic as chief. Can you tell the Court who Mr. Babic was and what was his role with in civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I see the signature as well, and I recognise it. This gentleman was an officer. I think he was either a colonel or a lieutenant-colonel at the time. He was assistant minister for defence and, at the same time, the head of civil protection as part of the ministry. Civil protection was within his remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if in the English we can go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, under item 2, it says: "Establish continuous duty rosters, and staff members are to take action especially on the following: Sheltering, evacuating, and providing treatment." Now, before I ask you my next question, let me go to another document, which is D256, and that one will appear on the screen shortly. You will see this is also a document from Mr. Babic from civil protection, this time dated 2 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, the document that we saw on our screen, there seems to be a cover page saying "Footnote 37," which, because it is a three-page document, of course I wonder to what it is a footnote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe, if you know, it comes from a Croatian government document that was produced. It's a study by the Croatian government which was produced to the OTP, and then there are footnotes to it. So these are the documents that referenced in the broader document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So perhaps for this document, then it is totally useless to have it be added as a footnote if we don't have the original. So, perhaps, we could it a two-page document in English, rather than a three-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It was a Defence exhibit, so we just used the same one rather than uploading a different version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We tendered it, but it is an OTP exhibit. All of these are from their 65 ter list, and they all have the footnote -- all the documents have the footnote page, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I now know what it is, and I'll not break my legs over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: We'll remove the first page, Your Honour, if the Defence agrees. It's a Defence exhibit so I have to ask their permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, now the document in front of you, before I stopped by questioning, is a 2 August from civil protection; and, here, we see once again item 1, sheltering; item 2; evacuation; and item 3, care. Now, can you please explain to the Court what the civilian population was supposed to do in case of an emergency or an attack, and let's start with the first item, in terms of sheltering?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: May I just offer a comment on the two documents? Am I allowed to do that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no problem in giving your comment, but I'd invite you first to answer the question that was put to you by Mr. Hedaraly. If there's anything you'd like to add, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that the second document stems from the first document covering some of the same issues. Hereby, the person drafting it is asking to see how the plans concerning sheltering and elevation, as well as care, are progressing. In the first case of sheltering, the civilians, in case of air-strikes, it is important that the population be sheltered in the existing facilities, as soon as possible. Some of the newer date buildings did have such, as call them, nuclear shelters; whereas, the older ones did not. Hence, people hid in cellars and rooms of that nature, and a plan was devised to what building people were supposed to go from their own respective buildings. It was important that, first, people are sheltered from any dangers of a possible attack, and they were supposed to cover a distance of between 50 and 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Okay. That is the first item, sheltering. Now, what about in terms of evacuation. What was the civilian population supposed to do in case of an emergency or an attack?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Evacuation is phase two. The civil protection was supposed to draw up plans, and we can see that it required materiel, supplies, and teams who were supposed to receive and accommodate the population. Also, the movement of people from the endangered -- from the area that is in danger was supposed to be undertaken, but not to a great distance. The distance involved was between ten and 20 kilometres. I think that was the distance mentioned in the plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, in 1995, had you seen any of the specific plans that had been prepared by civil protection?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That was outside of my remit and I had no occasion to see those plans; however, I do know that they were in existence. I was in close contact with the people responsible for it, specifically Mr. Babic and others. I do know that there were working on those plans and there was no reason for me to question that. Also, under the existing regulations, they were duty-bound to have such plans ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you D253 which is the evacuation plan for the municipality of Benkovac, and that is the municipality where you were born. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That`s going to come up on the screen soon. You have a hard copy of it in tab 4 of the -- of the documents you have in front of you, if you want to refer to the paper copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if, Mr. Registrar, we can go to page 2 of this document, and it's a chart so we can use only the B/C/S version for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Novakovic, let me first ask you: The villages on this chart, are they located roughly according to their geographical location relative to one another. By that, I mean, for example, Zagrad and Rastevic, are they to the west of Benkovac, and so on?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, therefore, is it fair to say that on this chart the front line is to the west and the south of the -- of this chart?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, on the left portion of this chart that we see page 2 of Exhibit D253, there is an curved line going from the top, and above it, there is a Roman numeral I. Do you know what that number represents?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It probably represents the first group of villages that was the closest to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, similarly, towards the middle of the page on the top, we see another curved line with a Roman numeral II this time. What would that indicate?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was another group of villages further away from the front line by some 15 up to 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, finally, we see a Roman numeral III as well, just under the line where there is the Roman numeral II line. So would that be a further group of villages even further removed?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One concludes that this would be the third group of villages in a relatively safe area removed from both the first and second area and the front line itself by some 30 or even more kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how this witness knows what those numbers mean on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You could ask the witness, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you know -- well, Mr. Novakovic, how do you know what these numbers represent?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It is very clear from the schematic. Since I had occasion to see these documents before I was shown these documents by the prosecutor, I was able to arrive at certain conclusions as to the meaning of the first, second, and third line. The first line encompasses all of the villages, such as Civljane, Smilcic, Biljane, Ceranje, and Kakma, and so on, these being the villages immediately adjacent to the front line. In the second group, you see some of the villages that are a bit further away, thus being included into the second group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Again, with respect to the foundation, if with could explore --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think, as we go through documents, the witness will clearly explain this in the rest of the document, and that is what I was going do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There are two issues: To explain the document and to explore the source of knowledge on why the document should be explained as the witness does. You may have an understanding of the substance of it, which does not necessarily include that you know what was in the mind of those who have drawn these lines --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was thinking along the lines of, was he personally in any way involved in these types of things so that he would know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think the answer was clear that he was not involved in a specific detail, he had the general understanding, and now I'm showing an example to see if that is assistant with his general understanding of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We could ask, "If you are not involved in drafting it, then, of course you could, as a citizen, it could be that you received it," or whatever; but would you please explore to the extent possible where the knowledge of the witness comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, your knowledge of these various steps or phases that we see on this evacuation plan that we've discussed, where does this knowledge come from that there were such phases?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the Military Academy specializing at the senior political school, and I have a Ph.D. in military science. Matters such as this one and many others are familiar to me. This is a relatively simply schematic although practical. Even a layperson would be able to conclude what it means. The person drafting this, or the group of people drafting this, included the villages from Benkovac municipality into the three groups represented. One can clear see that the first group represents the villages that are on the front line itself. The second group is between the first group, towards the interior of the country of the region by some 15 to 20 kilometres. The third group is even further removed by some five or eight kilometres, towards a territory that was not in the combat area, out of range of artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can then go to the next page of this document, page 3, and we can have the translation at the same time for this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: You see the top of this document says "First phase of the evacuation." Can you tell the Court what this page represents?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On this page, we see the villages that fall under Roman numeral I in the previous document. The first group is included in the first phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: It was only logical --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't mean to interrupt you. The people from these villages in phase one are supposed to go in case of an attack in Benkovac, Bijeljina, Kistanje. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Save for Kistanje, all the other villages are in Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can now go to page 7 of this exhibit in the B/C/S, and I believe it is page 9 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this time we have a similar chart again, but for what appears to be villages from the second phase. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, precisely from the group marked with Roman numeral II.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this time we see that the villages where people are supposed to go are Bijeljina, Dobropoljci, Bruska, Biovcino Selo, and Parcici. Right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. Expect for the village of Biovcino, all the others come under the Benkovac municipality; whereas, Biovcino falls under Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will ask you to show the Court where the villages are in a second. Let's just go through phase three quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is at page 11 of the B/C/S; page 14 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And this time we can see that these people from the phase three victims are supposed to go, once again, Bijeljina, Parcici, Kistanje, and Biovcino Selo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, let me just ask you, all of villages where people were supposed to go, generally speaking where were they located with respect to the town of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: The villages were located to the north-east of Benkovac by some 20 to 25 kilometres. If you follow the front line, it`s almost 40 kilometres, perhaps not as many, but roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 2 of the document, the chart that we had seen, the approximate map with all of villages listed on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And we can see on this some of the villages where people were supposed to go, so Parcici, Bijeljina, Dobropoljci, Bruska, are all located on the right-hand side of this chart in the top half. Do you see that on this chart?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we move a limited higher, we can see there is an arrow for Kistanje going to the right and an arrow to the top for, B. Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Which, Your Honour, the Prosecution assumes is Biovcino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is Kistanje in that direction to the east of this map, the north-east?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that the two were added. Biovcino and Kistanje was added by someone ineptly. Back in that table, you could see that the villages were included; whereas, they were not in this schematic. The schematic in itself is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, could you repeat, because it was not caught the transcriber. The Prosecution considered B. Selo to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Biovcino Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Biovcino. We found that where on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's on -- there is an arrow on the right -- there is an arrow to the right going to Kistanje and an arrow going north, B. Selo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Novakovic, Kistanje and Biovcino Selo, I think you said but I want to make sure, were not in the Benkovac municipality. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. They were in the municipality of Knin, Your Honours. Biovcino village lies on the boundary between the Knin and Benkovac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: All the other villages that we see on this chart are all in the Benkovac municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you see also, on this chart, there's is a broken line starting to the right of where the Roman numeral II is curving around and encompassing these villages. Do you know what that curved, broken line represents?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. Logically speaking, this is an area outside of the combat zone, out of the range of artillery fire, so I would conclude that it is a safe area; and my village, Bijeljina, is in the centre of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, to your knowledge as an assistant commander, did other municipalities have plans similar to this one?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Everyone had to have such or similar plans. Some had better plans, others poorer, but everyone had plans for their municipalities. In fact, they were mostly municipal level plans. That's who would produce them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And how long were the people that went to these safer villages supposed to say there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's a relatively issue, really; but definitely not too long. For instance, had the international community intervened on the 4th of August or in any other way, the population would have returned to the area quite soon, just as they had done previously when other events were happening. At any rate, the population did not embark on an elevation in order to stay in the area where they were evacuated permanently. The point was that they would return to their home settlements at a certain point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did any of these plans, did any of these municipalities contemplate people leaving permanently?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, again, to your knowledge, did any of those plans contemplate people leaving the territory of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: No, none of the plans did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Novakovic. I want to change topics and talk about the 4th of August, the attack that occurred. Can you briefly tell the Court what happened on the 4th, as early as you remember in the morning, and what were your personal observations in the morning on the 4th of August.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 4th of August, at 4.15 in the morning, I received information from the communications officer that I should report to the command as soon as possible, urgently, that I had a message from the UNPROFOR command from the UNPA zone where the Sector South command was located. I was in bed, so I dressed up in a hurry, and it took me perhaps some ten minutes to reach the command. The communications officer, who was a civilian, he was in charge of liaising the Main Staff, the government, and the Sector South command, as well as the UNPROFOR command in Zagreb. He told us that the Croatian army would most definitely attack us at 5.00. This was the information we had. We had all sorts of information circulating, ill-meant and well-meant, but let us not dwell on that now. I called my colleague who was the duty officer in the Main Staff to tell him that he should inform the corps commands, the senior officers who resided in Knin, and, above all, that he should call Commander Mrksic to come to the staff, to the headquarters. I think that he did everything that we agreed. For my part, I was thinking about where I was going to work because my office was in the army hall, which did not offer any sort of protection. It had transparent slabs on the roof, not a proper roof at all. Precisely at 0500 hours, heavy artillery fire started. I should say it started from all manner of weaponry. It was in salvos. There were multi-barrel rockets, and there were Howitzers, 155-millimetre, 120-millimetres -- or rather, it is 122. I believe that even tanks were active. My colleague and I found shelter under a staircase for a while and then proceed to an office that was relatively safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I could say that I was counting them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Well, let me first ask you: What were you counting?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Had I had occasion to count, I believe that in the first half-hour more than 500 rounds of shells of varying calibre landed on Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In the course of the morning and that day, when the attack took place, what was the atmosphere in the town or in the army hall or at any other location that you may have been?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I must say that, initially, in the army hall where I was present, there were only two or three people; but then they kept coming during the day, going to and fro throughout the day. Since the Main Staff was situated in the immediate proximity -- or rather, my office in the army hall was quite close to the Main Staff, so that during the day, I passed through that area by the building where the -- where General Mrksic's office was - it was some 50 metres - some 20 times a day. I know that, in my office, at times there were 15 people present, and I kept receiving different information. I don't know how descriptive I should be. I go only give you the gist, and then if you have questions, you can put them. In the course of the day, at 10.00, I had a meeting with my associates and UNPROFOR representatives: General Alan Forand, the commander; his chief for civilian affairs, I believe his name was Hussein Al-Alfi; Mr. Alun Roberts; and a dozen other officers, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And did you receive any reports as to which areas under attack or what was being targeted, either in Knin or in the RSK in general?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received reports from the commander and other people who came in with information. We had information to the effect that all the larger settlements were shelled at the time, all the villages. I have to say that settlements were more exposed to fire than were the units that were engaging the units of the Croatian army. That's why there was an impression made of the fact that there were suffered grave losses of people. In the first hours of the day, people were panic-stricken and started leaving. Out of the group of people who were with me in the press centre, some people who initially showed up eventually were no longer there. They decided to start leaving Knin. For instance, the population of Obrovac had moved out already at 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me move forward to the afternoon of the 4th, and we discussed some of the evacuation plans, i.e., the Benkovac plan, a few minutes ago. I want to show you D137, which is the actual decision that was taken by the Supreme Defence Council that were at least signed by President Martic, to evacuate the civilian population. That is going to come up on the screen in a few seconds. First of all, I want to ask you, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And why are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Because I authored the document, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the circumstances under which you authored this document -- actually, before I ask you that question - I'm sorry - there is a handwritten number on the top there, the number of the outgoing correspondence, I assume. Is that your handwriting that we see there?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me go back to the question I wanted to ask you. What are the -- can you tell us the circumstances under which you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: As one can see, the document was produced in the afternoon after 1600 hours. Let me just add that, previously, we had a meeting with the UNPROFOR command, who promised that they would intervene through the UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb, to ensure that civilian targets are not fired upon. In that period, we had contacts with our units, all the way through the afternoon hours. And at 1400 hours, I gave an interview from my office to for Radio Belgrade, and the information I had at that time was that our situation was relatively good in terms of the front lines not having moved at that time. However, already at this time, as the preamble of the document says, certain areas were endangered. Our unit which was on the Senj-Vrlika axis was threatened where our Vrbnik 1st Light Brigade was located. On the other hand, our units stationed on the western slope of Velebit at Mali Alan was threatened. That is where 4th Light Obrovac Brigade and 7th Dalmatia Corps were stationed, as well as the 7th Motorised Brigade from the 15th Lika Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me take you back to D137, the decision, and you said you authored it. Was that on your own initiative, or did someone ask you to prepare this.

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: I was just about to come to that point. At 1630 hours, General Mrksic summoned me and asked me what I was doing. He told me, "Why don't you come over so that we could see what we are going to do with the population, since it is at risk." President Martic was in my office; General Loncar, the Chief of Staff was there. He said also that there was one of the ministers there with him. Then Minister Kovacevic, the minister of information; and Knin mayor arrived. He said, We have to see what we're going to do next." I reached his office in less than two to three minutes. As I stepped into Mr. Mrksic's office, General Mrksic's office, I already found all the individuals I mentioned there. Mr. Mrksic then briefed us on the situation and said, literally, "President Martic spoke with Prime Minister Babic, who is in Belgrade. Babic, as we all know, attended the meeting with US Ambassador Peter Galbraith, and I think that Croatia will not stop." President Martic spoke with both Belgrade and Pale. My presumption was, although he didn't say that in so many words, that he spoke with Milosevic and Karadzic. I consulted minister -- the defence minister and the minister of the interior, because they, in addition to President Martic and commander, were members of the Supreme Defence Council. Then he said, "We decided that we ought to evacuate the population out of Dalmatia, Knin, Benkovac, Obrovac, and Drnis were the municipalities involved, and out of the Gracac municipality in Lika. Now why - I didn't finish this story - because there was the danger that practically, across Mali Alan, the route would be cut off, which was the only route leading toward the hinterland via Otocac. In Dalmatia, the army and the entire population would find themselves encircled. I do not wish to abuse your time. If need be, I can explain later on. But we now how the Serbian units and Serbian population -- what sort of end they met and what their fate was when they found themselves in encirclement. Let me go back to this decision. I was told that the population should move out or relocate to Otric and Srb -- or rather, via Oric, Srb, and Lapac, and that I should write a decision to that effect. They didn't explain this to me in great detail, but told me to see with the UNPROFOR command, since this was my part of the job, whether they could get involved in this. I went back into my office, I drafted this decision, and you can see that it was done in 1645 until 1710. So it took me some 20 minutes, half an hour. Why did I type this out on my own? Well, in order to make sure that a typist, typing it up, would not reek havoc. That's why I did it on myself, and that's why you have some typos there. I used an electrical typewriter -- no, I used a mechanical typewriter. I brought it over and the president signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me go back to something that you said in your answer about Mrksic telling you that the civilian population had to be saved. Was there any discussion in that meeting of the Croatian artillery attack on the region?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The attack was the main reason why the population needed to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 6113, and this is an extract from a book of Mr. Sekulic. It will come up on the screen shortly, and it is page 179 of his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page of that document in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The portion in the middle of the page in the B/C/S, the paragraph that starts rights with: "Decision of the Supreme Defence of Council communicated to the public at 2000 hours on 4 August. Then there is the next paragraph, which is the quote of that press release or communique, and I want to read that and ask you a question about it. It says: "During today's session, the Supreme Defence of Council of Republika Srpska Krajina delivered decision to organise the evacuation of the civilian population of Northern Dalmatia and the southern part of Lika, due to the preventative and security reasons. The members of the United Nations peace force, along with members of the RSK civilian protection, shall take active participation in the organisation of the evacuation and escort the civilian population." Now, I want to focus on this last sentence: "This decision of the Supreme Defence of Council has been delivered in order to protect the civilian population from any possible further attacks of the Croatian artillery, and in order for the Serb soldiers who are keeping the lines of defence to be relieved of worry for their families." My question for you is: Is this -- what we see in this report of a press release, is this consistent with the reasons why this decision was taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to note an objection. This is now impeaching the witness, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is consistent; it is not an impeachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It is impeachment. The witness has testified that there is was no announcement in the public about the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss this in the presence of the witness. Mr. Novakovic, do you understand the English language? It appears from the statements that you have some knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, yes, partly I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When we start discussing impeachment or not, either we do it in such a way by not by making reference to statement and lines without the witness immediately following it, or to do it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I simply asked him, generally, what his understanding of the meaning was, and I'm asking if is this consistent with what happened. I'm not attempting to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. Hedaraly, how much time would you still further need?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Twenty to 30 minutes; I'm hoping 20 will be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That couldn't be done before the break. Therefore, Mr. Novakovic, since a procedural issue has been raised, we would rather discuss this in your absence, which will give you some more time for a coffee break. Therefore, I suggest that we ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in approximately half an hour, Mr. Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see where are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My objection is at, P1092, page 11, the witness, his testimony is, because is it now 92 ter material, is: In the first full paragraph towards the middle, he talks about the evacuation order, and then says, "The decision was not forwarded through the official mail, and was not publicised through the media. Then the question posed to him is page -- page 36, line 16: "My question for you is: Is this what we see in this report of a press release?" Now, I consider those to be inconsistent with what they've put the witness to say: There was no public announcement of this. Now, they're putting it to him: Is the public announcement that was, in fact, put out in the public consistent with what you believe. I call the Trial Chamber's attention to the Appeals Chamber's decision in Popovic from the 1st of February, 2008, decision on appeals against decision on impeachment of a party's own witness, in which the Appeals Chamber said that a calling party must seek the permission of the Trial Chamber to impeach its own witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr., Hedaraly, apparently, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm obviously not trying to impeach my own witness. I think it is clear to everyone here that I am not. There is a document from another witness saying that it is a press release. I'm not confronting him by telling there was, No, there was press release, wasn't there? I'm asking whether the content of that release as it is stated in a book that the Defence is trying to introduce, a portion which is in evidence, which is in one of pages. I'm asking him whether this is consistent with the reasons that he was given for drafting the actual decision. I am more than happy to explore with him the matter, or if Mr. Misetic wants to in cross-examination, as to his knowledge of who issued the press release, if someone else may have done it. And, further, the fact that he did not issue himself a press release or didn't know about it does not mean that it didn't occur. But that is not the main point of my question, and I think I was hoping that it was clearer. But if there's a way that Your Honour you want to assist me in asking the question to make it clearer, so that I'm not questioning his statement that there was or there was not a press release, but focussing on the contents of it, as to the reasons why the decision was given to evacuate the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is improper on direct. He has already put to him what was said at the meeting, was there a decision about artillery. He can put him whatever else he wants in terms of what his specific issue are. But what appears to be happening, then, is to say, Well, now we would like to stick this book page in front of the Trial Chamber and have the witness tell the Trial Chamber whether what's in a book is consistent with what he just told the Trial Chamber. I'm sure the Trial Chamber will be able, particularly after cross-examination, to evaluate whether it is consistent or not. But we don't need to go through the exercise again, particularly where it is now muddying the waters as to whether there was a public announcement, which is what Mr. Sekulic says in the book; or there wasn't, which what the witness is now testified to before the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, do I understand that whether it was publicly announced is not the issue, but we're, rather, talking about the substance?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if that's the issue, and not the public announcement, why not ask the witness something in general terms, that the order was once described by someone as so-and-so and so, does that fit? I mean, apparently, if it is about the substance, then whether the substance is presented in a certain context, apparently the context is not what you're seeking. So let's then focus on the substance entirely and leave out the context. Is that a solution? Because then the issue of impeaching your own witness disappears.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think that is my point, Your Honour. He has already said that there was this discussion about artillery at the meeting, so I don't know what the point of the exercise is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have two issues: First of all, whether Mr. Hedaraly is at the point of impeaching the witness. I think I gave some guidance as at least how to avoid that element; then, of course, what then follows is whether there's any reputation in the question. Mr. Hedaraly, you have 25 minutes to think about the question of how to phrase it or rephrase it, to avoid repetition and to, from what I understand, so that the issue which caused Mr. Misetic to talk about it impeachment is not an issue you want to cover at this moment. So if you refrain from touching upon that, then Mr. Misetic will have no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: One other objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I object to the English translation on the screen for some. For some reason, only a selected portions has been extracted from the page on the screen, and we have a complete translation of the page which puts it back into the context of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That raises a very interesting issue. Your Honour a while ago instructed the parties to agree. The Defence moved in to chapters of this book, and Chamber instructed the Prosecution and the Defence would agree on specific pages to be admitted to an exhibit. In Exhibit D260, the Defence had page 180 and 181. The Prosecution has now repeatedly ask the Defence to add page 179 and their translation to D260, but for some reason it is still not done. So we have to have our own translation and upload it, and that's why this issue arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This again is an issue, whether true or not, I see some body language, someone nodding no, other perhaps nodding yes. It appears to me to be a matter which if it is just as practical, as Mr. Hedaraly says, I think it could be resolved quickly. If it is not that, the Chamber would like to hear either now or after the break what remains as a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We'll talk about it, Your Honour. I think our position has been clear all along. We want the whole section of the book that deals with Operation Storm, and the Prosecution now wants to piecemeal it. We'll talk about it during the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that. There is also an issue of uploading the translation, which apparently you don't have the full translation of everything, and you are seeking --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, no. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr Hedaraly mention that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I will discuss it with Mr. Misetic at the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be a good idea. Then I have to admit that where I usually insist on precision, that I'm only one week wrong, at least my agenda, and I leave it alone who put it in my agenda, but the swearing-in ceremony is for the 20th not the 13th, although it appears in my agenda, which caused me to announce that we would have an early finish today. That was totally wrong, and we will just go on until quarter to 2.00. But you're already on notice that next week, I don't know whether we're sitting in the morning or the afternoon, but if we're sitting in the morning, we will have an early break; if we are sitting in the afternoon, we likely will have a late start. There is one other small matter, and that is, Mr. Misetic, the objection of the Defence against the two documents which are now marked for identification included an objection against having it admitted to the 65 ter list. By marking it for identification, that was more or less ignored. Would you like to further argue on whether or not it should even be admitted to the 65 ter list, or would it be sufficient for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No, that's fine, Your Honour. If it is already MFI'd, that's fine. I would like to have the opportunity to discuss that with counsel. My issue, now that the witness is not here, is I believe it is undisputed between the Prosecution and the Defence that there are certain elements of map that are just wrong, and units that never existed in Operation Storm, which is I wanted to get at what his underlying foundation is, and I don't think that those are issues in dispute between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If not, of course, then a solution is at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Novakovic, I would like to thank you. I see that you have produced the CD. Let me just try to decipher the literature, if I read your Cyrillic well, the literature you used. The parties, of course, will have it now available and can further work with it, if they wish to do so. Thank you very much, Mr. Novakovic. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes. On the matter of the book, I have discussed with Mr. Misetic, and we're essentially saying similar things. There was an exhibit tendered by the Defence, or referred to by the Defence, which was two chapters of that book, 93 pages, dealing with Operation Storm. At the time, the Prosecution wanted to review to make sure those were, in fact, relevant. Later on with another witness, when another portion of that collection was used, once again the Prosecution did not force any objection to Defence exhibit, but the Chamber expressed concerns of having 93 pages, which may not all be used by witnesses, and that's where we stand now. Mr. Misetic told me that most of these 93 pages, or a significant portion of it, will be used with some witnesses. This is the only page, page 179, that the Prosecution intends to use from those 93 pages. But at this point, for the sake of convenience, we still don't have any objection to the full two chapters being in evidence. But, of course, if the Chamber wants individual pages as they are being used with the witnesses, we will abide by that instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What the Chamber seeks is to have the relevant portions in an understandable context to be presented. That context often would not require more than one or two pages, but it's not to be said that that is always the case. Context is to be considered on a case by case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is the way the way the book is structured is they are -- it is a compilation of the reports of the individual officers of the RSK, for each unit, during Operation Storm. And, as such, it is not only a book, but it is a compilation of individual reports. All of it, we believe, is relevant. You've now see, for example, a map tendered by the Prosecution this morning about locations of various ARSK and HV positions, as well as their recollections of what happened with their unit in their area of responsibility on the day in question. We will be and have been going back and forth throughout those two chapters of the book. We believe that, for the sake of convenience, they should be in one location, rather than chopping them up. The second portion of it is, Your Honour, to the extent that there are certain pages that aren't used, this may be an exhibit that is a combination used live with witnesses and partially bar table. But, overall, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, I earlier said to have the relevant portions in an understandable context. Sometimes, portions come so close and are so many that to create a context would be to present the whole chapter or the whole chapters. What the Chamber wants to avoid is that we get a lot of pages which have hardly any at all -- any relevance at all. That is, of course, what we want to avoid; not to prevent the parties from putting relevant material, even if one page or one and a half or two or three pages would not be very relevant, but would be part of a chapter which is, as a whole, very relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I leave, at this moment, to the parties to agree on that. Of course, I do now understand, Mr. Hedaraly, that there is no objection against what you intend to do. So lets then do it, and, of course, it has the advantages of not chopping up in tiny little parts the evidence where we have to read separate pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Also, just as a practical matter, the translation is already -- has been uploaded, so there is no translation issues for those 93 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So that was a mistake. Let's then proceed. I would say, you have had, apart from conversations with Mr. Misetic, you had 30 minutes to think about your question, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Novakovic, before the break, I showed you a statement made by someone, and I'll repeat just the last sentence of it, which is: "The Supreme Defence Council made this decision," the one to evacuate the civilians, "in order to protect the civilian population from possible further Croatian artillery attacks, and to spare the Serbian soldier who is are holding the lines of defence from anxiety about their families." My question is: Is that consistent with the reasons you were given at your meeting with Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Martic as to why this decision was made?

utterances.speaker: KOSTA NOVAKOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And I don't know if I should tender this page, Your Honour, or simply wait for --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will tender -- I can tender it now it now or when we are in the Defence case. It doesn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It is just page 179 that we want, but if the whole -- it is part of that collection of 93 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it is now on the record that it will be included in the portions of the book that the Defence will tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go back now to D137, the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: This is the decision that you drafted, and let me -- I want to draw your attention, when it comes up on the screen, to point number 2.
